Chapter 2: Getting Started with Scratch (Block-Based Coding)

 

Section 1: Introduction to Scratch Interface and Features

What’s Scratch All About?

Scratch is like the ultimate starter kit for coding, created by the smart folks at MIT (a super cool tech school). It’s a free, online tool where you can make interactive stories, animations, and games by snapping together blocks—no typing, no complicated stuff, just pure creativity! It’s perfect for high schoolers like you because it lets you focus on the ideas behind coding (like logic and problem-solving) without worrying about spelling errors or weird symbols. Over 70 million people worldwide use Scratch, and there are millions of projects to explore—everything from hilarious memes to epic adventure games. You’re joining a huge, creative community!

Why Start with Scratch?

Think of Scratch as training wheels for coding. It helps you understand how coding works in a visual, hands-on way before you dive into text-based languages like Python or JavaScript later in this course. Plus, it’s insanely fun—you can make a character do a backflip or say something goofy in just a few clicks. Scratch also teaches you big coding concepts (like loops and if-statements) that are used in every programming language, so you’re building real skills while having a blast. And hey, if you’ve ever dreamed of making a viral game or animation, Scratch is where tons of teens start!

Getting to Know the Scratch Interface

Let’s take a tour of Scratch so you feel right at home. Head over to on your browser (no download needed!), click “Join Scratch” to make a free account (use a cool username!), and then click “Create” to start a new project. Here’s what you’ll see on your screen:

  • Stage (Top Right): This is like your project’s TV screen—it’s where your creations come to life. Anything you code will play out here, like a character moving or speaking. It’s 480x360 pixels (kinda like a mini YouTube video frame).
  • Sprite List (Bottom Right): Sprites are your characters or objects (like a cat, ball, or spaceship). This area shows all the sprites in your project. Scratch starts you with a cute cat named “Sprite1,” but you can add more from their library or draw your own.
  • Costumes Tab (Next to Sprite List): Think of this as your sprite’s wardrobe. You can change how a sprite looks—like making the cat wear sunglasses or turn into a zombie. Each “costume” is a different look for the same sprite.
  • Blocks Palette (Left Side): This is your toolbox! It’s full of colorful blocks you drag and drop to code. Categories like “Motion” (move stuff), “Looks” (change appearance), “Sound” (play music), and “Events” (make things happen) are here. Each block does something specific, like “move 10 steps” or “say ‘Hi!’ for 2 seconds.”
  • Coding Area (Middle): This is where the magic happens. Drag blocks from the palette and snap them together here to tell your sprite what to do. It’s like building a puzzle—blocks only fit if they make sense together.
  • Green Flag & Stop Buttons (Above Stage): The green flag starts your project (like hitting “play” on a video), and the red stop sign pauses it. Use these to test what you’ve made as you go.

    •  

Cool Features to Explore

Scratch is packed with stuff to make your projects pop. Here are a few features that’ll get you excited:

  • Sprite Library: Click the “Choose a Sprite” button (little cat icon below the stage) to pick from hundreds of characters—robots, dinosaurs, even pizza slices! You can also upload your own pics (like a selfie or meme) to make custom sprites.
  • Backdrop Library: Click the “Choose a Backdrop” button (landscape icon) to set a background for your stage—like a space galaxy, basketball court, or haunted house. It sets the vibe for your story or game.
  • Sound Effects: Add music or funny noises (like a “boing!” or rap beat) from the “Sounds” tab. You can even record your own voice—imagine your sprite rapping your latest TikTok sound!
  • Paint Editor: Draw your own sprites or edit existing ones with Scratch’s built-in drawing tool. Make a stick figure of your bestie or doodle a weird monster—it’s all up to you.

Teen Tip: Make It Yours!

Spend 5 minutes exploring the interface. Click random blocks, drag them around, and see what happens when you press the green flag. Don’t worry about “breaking” anything—Scratch is all about experimenting! For extra fun, pick a sprite and backdrop that match your vibe (like a skatepark with a cool skater sprite if you’re into skating). Feeling stuck? Scratch has built-in tutorials (click “Tutorials” at the top) with quick videos—perfect for visual learners like most teens.

Fun Fact

Did you know Scratch was launched in 2007 and is named after “scratching” in hip-hop (like DJs mixing sounds)? Just like DJs remix tracks, you’ll remix ideas and blocks to create something totally new. How cool is that?

 

Section 2: Creating Your First Project: Simple Animations

Let’s Make Something Move!

Now that you know your way around Scratch, let’s create your first project—an animation! Animations are like mini-movies where characters move, talk, or change looks. We’ll make the default Scratch Cat do a little dance and say something funny. This will teach you how to use blocks and test your ideas. Ready? Let’s go!

Step-by-Step: Dancing Cat Animation with Coding Steps

  • Start a New Project: Go to , log in, and click “Create.” You’ll see the Scratch Cat (Sprite1) on a blank stage.
  • Make the Cat Move: In the Blocks Palette, click the “Motion” category (blue blocks). Drag the “move 10 steps” block to the Coding Area. Click the block directly to test it—see the cat slide forward on the stage? Change “10” to “50” by typing in the box for a bigger move. Drag it back with “move -50 steps” (negative numbers move left).
  • Start with a Trigger: Click the “Events” category (yellow blocks). Drag the “when green flag clicked” block to the Coding Area and snap it above your “move” blocks. This tells Scratch to run your code when you hit the green flag (like saying “Action!” on a movie set).
  • Add a Dance Loop: Click “Control” (orange blocks) and grab the “repeat 10” block. Wrap it around your “move 50 steps” and “move -50 steps” blocks by dragging them inside the loop’s “C” shape. This repeats the back-and-forth 10 times, like a dance! Test it by clicking the green flag—your cat should shimmy!
  • Make It Talk: Go to “Looks” (purple blocks) and drag “say ‘Hello!’ for 2 seconds.” Snap it under your loop. Change “Hello!” to something funny like “I’m a dance machine!” Test it—the cat should talk after dancing.
  • Add Flair with Costumes: Click the “Costumes” tab for the cat. You’ll see different poses (like “cat-a” and “cat-b”). Back in “Looks,” grab the “switch costume to cat-b” block and add it after “move 50 steps.” Add “switch costume to cat-a” after “move -50 steps.” Now your cat changes poses while dancing—like flipping arms or legs!
  • Save and Name It: Click “File” > “Save to your computer” or save it online if logged in. Name it “Dancing Cat Remix” or something cool. Congrats—you’ve made your first animation!

    •  

Final Code Sequence for Dancing Cat Animation

  • Events: “when green flag clicked”
  • Control: “repeat 10”
    • Motion: “move 50 steps”
    • Looks: “switch costume to cat-b”
    • Motion: “move -50 steps”
    • Looks: “switch costume to cat-a”
  • Looks: “say ‘I’m a dance machine!’ for 2 seconds”

Why This Matters

This simple project teaches you three huge coding ideas: sequencing (putting blocks in order to do things step-by-step), events (starting actions with triggers like the green flag), and repetition (using loops to repeat moves). Plus, you’ve just turned an idea into something real—how awesome is that? Animations are a great way to express yourself, whether you’re making a funny skit for friends or a short story for class.

Teen Challenge: Personalize Your Animation

Make this animation yours! Swap the cat for a sprite you like (maybe a dinosaur or basketball player from the library). Change the backdrop to match (like a jungle or court). Edit the “say” block to something you’d post on socials—like “Bet you can’t dance like this!” Add a sound from the “Sound” tab (like a drumbeat) to play during the dance. Spend 10 minutes tweaking it, then show a friend or family member. Bet they’ll be impressed!

Real Teen Story

Meet Jayden, a 15-year-old from Texas. He started with Scratch last year and made a simple animation of a dog “talking” trash about homework (voiced by Jayden himself!). He shared it with his class, and everyone cracked up. Now he’s hooked and makes weekly animations for his school’s meme page. Your first project could be the start of something big too!

 

Section 3: Understanding Loops, Conditionals, and Variables in Scratch

Coding Concepts Made Easy

Now that you’ve made something cool, let’s level up by learning three building blocks of coding: loops, conditionals, and variables. These sound fancy, but Scratch makes them super simple with visual blocks. They’re like the secret sauce that turns basic projects into interactive, dynamic creations. Let’s break them down with practical examples you can try right now!

Loops: Repeat the Fun

What Are Loops? Loops tell your program to repeat actions over and over without you dragging the same block a million times. It’s like setting a playlist on repeat—same song, multiple plays. Example in Scratch: In your Dancing Cat project, you used the “repeat 10” block to make the cat dance back and forth 10 times. Without a loop, you’d have to copy-paste “move 50 steps” and “move -50 steps” 10 times each—boring! Try It with Coding Steps: Open a new project. Pick a sprite (like a bird). Follow these steps to make it fly endlessly:

  • From “Events,” drag “when green flag clicked” to the Coding Area.
  • From “Motion,” drag “go to x:0 y:0” and snap it under the event block to start at the center.
  • From “Control,” drag a “forever” loop and snap it under “go to.”
  • Inside the “forever” loop, add “glide 1 secs to x:100 y:0” (flies right).
  • Add another “glide 1 secs to x:-100 y:0” (flies left) under the first glide. Final Code Sequence for Bird Loop:
  • Events: “when green flag clicked”
  • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
  • Control: “forever”
    • Motion: “glide 1 secs to x:100 y:0”
    • Motion: “glide 1 secs to x:-100 y:0” Hit the green flag—your bird flies side to side forever! Loops save time and make animations smooth. Teen Twist: Add a “play sound ‘chirp’ until done” block inside the loop. Now your bird chirps as it flies—perfect for annoying your sibling with endless bird noises!

Conditionals: Make Decisions

What Are Conditionals? Conditionals are like “if-then” rules—they let your program make choices based on what’s happening. Think of it as deciding “If it’s raining, then I’ll grab an umbrella.” Example in Scratch: Let’s make a sprite react to your clicks. Pick a sprite (like a dog). Follow these steps:

  • From “Events,” drag “when this sprite clicked” to the Coding Area.
  • From “Looks,” snap “say ‘Woof! You got me!’ for 2 seconds” under it. Final Code Sequence for Click Reaction:
  • Events: “when this sprite clicked”
  • Looks: “say ‘Woof! You got me!’ for 2 seconds” Test it—click the dog, and it talks! This is an “if” condition: if clicked, then speak. Try It with More Logic: Add more logic with “if-else” from “Control.” Follow these steps:
  • Drag “when green flag clicked” from “Events.”
  • Drag an “if-else” block from “Control” under it.
  • From “Sensing,” grab “mouse down?” and place it in the diamond slot of “if.”
  • Add “say ‘Clicking somewhere!’ for 1 sec” in the “if” part.
  • Add “say ‘Not clicking!’ for 1 sec” in the “else” part. Final Code Sequence for Mouse Check:
  • Events: “when green flag clicked”
  • Control: “if <mouse down?> then”
    • Looks: “say ‘Clicking somewhere!’ for 1 sec”
  • else
    • Looks: “say ‘Not clicking!’ for 1 sec” Test it—your sprite reacts based on your action! Teen Twist: Change the messages to something funny like “Yo, stop clicking!” and “Finally, some peace!” Conditionals make projects interactive—great for games or pranks.

Variables: Keep Track of Stuff

What Are Variables? Variables are like storage boxes for info (like scores, names, or numbers) that can change as your project runs. It’s like tracking your high score in a game—it updates when you play better. Example in Scratch: Let’s make a click counter. Pick a sprite. Follow these steps:

  • Go to “Variables” (orange blocks), click “Make a Variable,” name it “Clicks,” and click OK.
  • From “Events,” drag “when green flag clicked.”
  • Drag “set Clicks to 0” from “Variables” under it to start at zero.
  • From “Events,” drag “when this sprite clicked” to a new stack.
  • Under it, add “change Clicks by 1” from “Variables.”
  • Add “say [Clicks] for 1 second” (use the “join” block from “Operators” to show the number by joining “Clicks” with an empty space or text). Final Code Sequence for Click Counter:
  • Stack 1:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Variables: “set Clicks to 0”
  • Stack 2:
    • Events: “when this sprite clicked”
    • Variables: “change Clicks by 1”
    • Looks: “say [join Clicks ‘’] for 1 sec” Test it—click the sprite, and it counts how many times! Try It with Conditional: Add a conditional to react to many clicks:
  • Under “when this sprite clicked,” after “change Clicks by 1,” add an “if” block from “Control.”
  • From “Operators,” drag “>” and set it to “Clicks > 5” in the “if” condition.
  • Add “say ‘Wow, you’re click-crazy!’ for 1 sec” inside the “if.” Updated Code Sequence for Click Counter with Conditional:
  • Stack 1:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Variables: “set Clicks to 0”
  • Stack 2:
    • Events: “when this sprite clicked”
    • Variables: “change Clicks by 1”
    • Looks: “say [join Clicks ‘’] for 1 sec”
    • Control: “if <Clicks > 5> then”
      • Looks: “say ‘Wow, you’re click-crazy!’ for 1 sec” Variables track data, making projects dynamic. Teen Twist: Turn it into a challenge—tell friends to get to 10 clicks fastest. Variables are key for games (like scores) or apps (like tracking steps).

Why These Matter to You

Loops, conditionals, and variables are the heart of coding—they let you create projects that repeat actions, react to users, and store info. Whether you’re making a game, quiz, or story, these concepts give you power to build stuff that feels alive. Plus, they’re used in every coding language, so learning them now in Scratch sets you up for Python or JavaScript later!

Interactive Challenge

Create a mini-project combining all three: Make a sprite (like a ghost) float up and down forever (loop), say “Boo!” if you click it (conditional), and count how many times you’ve scared it (variable). Add a funny backdrop like a graveyard. Follow these steps:

  • Create a variable “Scares” in “Variables.”
  • For floating: Use “when green flag clicked,” “go to x:0 y:0,” then a “forever” loop with “change y by 10” and “change y by -10” (add “wait 0.5 secs” between for smooth motion).
  • For clicking: Use “when this sprite clicked,” “say ‘Boo!’ for 1 sec,” and “change Scares by 1.” Final Code Sequence for Ghost Project:
  • Stack 1:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Variables: “set Scares to 0”
    • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
    • Control: “forever”
      • Motion: “change y by 10”
      • Control: “wait 0.5 secs”
      • Motion: “change y by -10”
      • Control: “wait 0.5 secs”
  • Stack 2:
    • Events: “when this sprite clicked”
    • Looks: “say ‘Boo!’ for 1 sec”
    • Variables: “change Scares by 1” Share it with a friend—see who can “scare” the ghost more times in 30 seconds!

 

Section 4: Building a Basic Game in Scratch (e.g., Maze or Pong)

Time to Build a Game!

You’ve got the basics down, so let’s create something you can play—a simple Pong game! Pong is a classic where a ball bounces between two paddles, and you score by getting past your opponent. It’s perfect for learning game design in Scratch, and you can play it with a friend. This project pulls together everything you’ve learned (motion, conditionals, variables) and adds game logic. Let’s make it step by step!

Step-by-Step: Creating Pong with Coding Steps

  • Set Up the Scene: Start a new project on Scratch. Choose a plain backdrop (like “Blue Sky”). Add two paddle sprites—use rectangles from the Paint Editor (draw tall, thin shapes) or pick something like “Paddle” from the library. Name them “Paddle1” (left) and “Paddle2” (right). Add a ball sprite (like “Ball” from the library or draw a circle).
  • Position the Paddles: For Paddle1, drag it to the left side of the stage. In “Motion,” use the following code to lock its starting spot:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Motion: “go to x:-200 y:0” Do the same for Paddle2:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Motion: “go to x:200 y:0” This sets up the “court.”
  • Control Paddles with Keys: For Paddle1, add movement controls:
    • Stack 1:
      • Events: “when up arrow key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by 10”
    • Stack 2:
      • Events: “when down arrow key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by -10” For Paddle2, use different keys:
    • Stack 1:
      • Events: “when w key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by 10”
    • Stack 2:
      • Events: “when s key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by -10” Test it—press keys to move paddles!
  • Make the Ball Move: For the Ball sprite, add code to move continuously:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
    • Control: “forever”
      • Motion: “move 5 steps”
      • Motion: “if on edge, bounce” This makes the ball zip around and bounce off walls. Adjust speed by changing “5” if it’s too fast/slow.
  • Bounce Off Paddles: Still on the Ball, inside the “forever” loop, add conditions for bouncing:
    • Inside “forever” loop, add:
      • Control: “if <touching Paddle1?> then”
        • Motion: “turn 180 degrees”
      • Control: “if <touching Paddle2?> then”
        • Motion: “turn 180 degrees” Test it—ball should bounce off paddles!
  • Score Points: Make two variables in “Variables”—“Score1” (for Paddle1) and “Score2” (for Paddle2). Add scoring logic:
    • For Ball sprite, under “when green flag clicked,” before the “forever” loop:
      • Variables: “set Score1 to 0”
      • Variables: “set Score2 to 0”
    • Inside the “forever” loop, after paddle checks, add:
      • Control: “if <x position > 240> then”
        • Variables: “change Score1 by 1”
        • Looks: “say ‘Point for Player 1!’ for 1 sec”
        • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
      • Control: “if <x position < -240> then”
        • Variables: “change Score2 by 1”
        • Looks: “say ‘Point for Player 2!’ for 1 sec”
        • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0” Test it—scores update!
  • Polish It: Add a “Broadcast” when a point is scored to play a sound:
    • Inside each “if” for scoring, add:
      • Events: “broadcast ‘point’”
    • Add a new sprite (or use Ball) with:
      • Events: “when I receive ‘point’”
      • Sound: “play sound ‘pop’ until done” Display scores on stage by checking “Show” for the variables in the Variables menu. Name your project “Epic Pong Battle” and save it.

Final Code Sequence for Pong Game

  • Paddle1:
    • Stack 1:
      • Events: “when green flag clicked”
      • Motion: “go to x:-200 y:0”
    • Stack 2:
      • Events: “when up arrow key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by 10”
    • Stack 3:
      • Events: “when down arrow key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by -10”
  • Paddle2:
    • Stack 1:
      • Events: “when green flag clicked”
      • Motion: “go to x:200 y:0”
    • Stack 2:
      • Events: “when w key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by 10”
    • Stack 3:
      • Events: “when s key pressed”
      • Motion: “change y by -10”
  • Ball:
    • Stack 1:
      • Events: “when green flag clicked”
      • Variables: “set Score1 to 0”
      • Variables: “set Score2 to 0”
      • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
      • Control: “forever”
        • Motion: “move 5 steps”
        • Motion: “if on edge, bounce”
        • Control: “if <touching Paddle1?> then”
          • Motion: “turn 180 degrees”
        • Control: “if <touching Paddle2?> then”
          • Motion: “turn 180 degrees”
        • Control: “if <x position > 240> then”
          • Variables: “change Score1 by 1”
          • Looks: “say ‘Point for Player 1!’ for 1 sec”
          • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
          • Events: “broadcast ‘point’”
        • Control: “if <x position < -240> then”
          • Variables: “change Score2 by 1”
          • Looks: “say ‘Point for Player 2!’ for 1 sec”
          • Motion: “go to x:0 y:0”
          • Events: “broadcast ‘point’”
    • Stack 2 (for sound, if separate):
      • Events: “when I receive ‘point’”
      • Sound: “play sound ‘pop’ until done”

Why Games Are Awesome to Build

Games like Pong teach you how to combine coding ideas—motion for movement, conditionals for collisions, variables for scores. Plus, they’re interactive, so you get instant feedback (and bragging rights when you beat a friend!). Game design is a huge career field—think of Fortnite or Roblox—and Scratch is where many game devs start.

Teen Challenge: Customize Your Pong

Make your Pong stand out! Change paddle sprites to something funny (like a banana or your fave character). Add a crazy backdrop (like “Space”). Increase ball speed after each point by adding a “Speed” variable (start at 5, increase by 1 per point). Play a round with a friend—who’s the Pong champ? Post a screenshot on socials with #MyPongGame to show off!

Fun Fact

The original Pong game from 1972 was one of the first video games ever made! It was so simple—just two paddles and a dot—but it started the gaming industry. Your Scratch Pong is following in legendary footsteps!

 

Section 5: Sharing and Collaborating on Scratch Projects

Show Off Your Creations!

You’ve built animations and a game—now let’s share them with the world! Scratch isn’t just a tool; it’s a community where millions of creators (many your age) share projects, give feedback, and remix each other’s work. Sharing is a great way to get inspired, learn new tricks, and even make online friends who love coding as much as you do. Plus, showing your projects can boost your confidence and maybe even impress a teacher or future college!

How to Share on Scratch

  • Save Your Project: Make sure your project (like your Dancing Cat or Pong) is saved. If you’re logged in, click “Save Now” to store it online in your Scratch account.
  • Publish It: At the top of the project editor, click the “Share” button. This makes your project public on the Scratch website so others can see and play it. Don’t worry—you can unshare later if you change your mind.
  • Add Details: Before sharing, give your project a cool name (like “Ultimate Dance Party” or “Pong Showdown”). Add a short description in the “Instructions” box (e.g., “Click to make the cat dance!”) and “Notes and Credits” (like “Thanks to my BFF for the idea!”). Tag it with keywords like “animation” or “game” so others can find it.
  • Share the Link: Once shared, you’ll get a unique link (like scratch.mit.edu/projects/123456). Copy it and send it to friends via text, Discord, or social media. You can also embed it in a blog or school site if you have one!
  • Explore the Community: Click “Explore” on Scratch’s homepage to see trending projects. Comment on ones you like (e.g., “Love the graphics!”) and click “Favorite” or “Love” to save them. You’ll get notifications if people comment on yours too!

Remixing: Build on Others’ Ideas

One of Scratch’s coolest features is “remixing”—taking someone else’s project and adding your own spin. Click “See Inside” on a shared project, then “Remix” to make a copy you can edit. Maybe add a new character, change the music, or tweak the rules of a game. Always give credit in the “Notes and Credits” section (e.g., “Remixed from @username’s awesome game!”). It’s like collabing on a TikTok dance—everyone adds their flavor! Here’s how to remix with a small coding tweak:

  • Open a shared project you like (e.g., a simple animation).
  • Click “Remix” to create your version.
  • Add a new feature, like a sound effect:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Sound: “play sound ‘cheer’ until done”
  • Save and share your remixed version with credit to the original creator.

Collaborating with Friends

Got a coding buddy? Work together! Scratch lets you share projects privately before publishing by sending the link while it’s unshared (or use “Backpack” to copy sprites/blocks between projects). Plan a project with a friend—like a story where you each animate a character. Meet up online or in person to brainstorm. Two heads are better than one, and you’ll learn from each other’s ideas. Some teens even form “Scratch Studios” (like group pages) to team up on big projects—search “Studios” on Scratch to join one! Here’s a quick way to collab with coding steps:

  • Create a joint project, like a dialogue between two sprites.
  • Assign one sprite to each person. For example, Sprite1 (handled by you):
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Looks: “say ‘Hey, what’s up?’ for 2 secs”
    • Control: “wait 2 secs”
    • Events: “broadcast ‘reply’”
  • Your friend codes Sprite2:
    • Events: “when I receive ‘reply’”
    • Looks: “say ‘Not much, you?’ for 2 secs”
  • Save and test together, tweaking the timing or messages as needed.

Safety First

Scratch is teen-friendly, but keep it chill online. Don’t share personal info (like your real name or address) in projects or comments. If someone’s rude, click “Report” on their comment or profile. Stick to fun, positive vibes—think of it like posting on Insta or Snap, but for coding. Your Scratch account is your creative space, so protect it!

Teen Challenge: Share and Remix

Share your favorite project from this chapter (animation or Pong) on Scratch. Write a fun description (e.g., “Can you beat my high score in Pong?”). Then, find a simple game or animation in “Explore,” remix it with one new feature (like a sound or extra sprite), and share your remix. Comment on the original to thank the creator. See if you get likes or comments—maybe you’ll go viral in the Scratch world! Here’s a quick remix idea with code:

  • Open a shared animation project via “See Inside” and click “Remix.”
  • Add a new sprite (like a bird) from the library.
  • Code the new sprite to react:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Motion: “go to x:100 y:100”
    • Control: “forever”
      • Motion: “change x by 5”
      • Motion: “if on edge, bounce”
  • Save and share with a note crediting the original creator.

Real Teen Story

Aaliyah, a 14-year-old from New York, shared her first Scratch game (a dodge-the-asteroids challenge) last summer. It got over 100 views and a dozen comments saying “So fun!” She remixed a fan’s suggestion to add power-ups, and now they collab on new levels together. Sharing turned her hobby into a friendship—and her game’s at 500 views now! Your shared project could be the start of something amazing.

Why Sharing Rocks

Sharing isn’t just showing off—it’s learning. Feedback teaches you what works (or doesn’t), remixing sparks new ideas, and collaborating builds teamwork skills (great for school or future jobs). Plus, having a Scratch portfolio shows off your creativity—imagine linking it in a college app or showing it at a tech club. You’re not just coding; you’re building a digital footprint of awesome!

 

 

Chapter Wrap-up

Wow, what a ride! In Chapter 2, you’ve gone from Scratch newbie to creating animations, understanding coding basics (loops, conditionals, variables), building a playable Pong game, and sharing your work with a global community. You’ve learned that coding isn’t just instructions—it’s creativity, logic, and fun all rolled into one. Scratch has given you a taste of what’s possible, and you’re just getting started!

Keep the Momentum

Before we move to Chapter 3 (where we’ll explore text-based coding with Python), take a moment to celebrate. Pick your favorite project from this chapter and play it one more time—smile at what you made! Then, jot down one idea for a bigger Scratch project (like a multi-level game or a full story with multiple characters). We’ll revisit these ideas later to see how far you’ve come. If you’re itching to add one last coding touch, try this mini-challenge:

  • Open your Pong game or animation.
  • Add a celebratory effect when the game starts:
    • Events: “when green flag clicked”
    • Sound: “play sound ‘cheer’ until done”
    • Looks: “say ‘Let’s go!’ for 1 sec”
  • Save and play one last time to enjoy your creation.

Quick Reflection Activity

Think about one thing you found tricky in Scratch (maybe loops or getting the ball to bounce right in Pong). Write down how you figured it out—or if you’re still stuck, ask a friend or check Scratch forums. Also, note one thing you’re proud of (like a funny animation line). Reflecting helps you grow as a coder!

Final Pep Talk

Remember, every game developer, app creator, and tech innovator started with small steps like these. Mistakes are your teachers (debugging is half the fun!), and every block you snap together builds your skills. You’ve got a community in Scratch—and in this course—to cheer you on. Keep experimenting, keep sharing, and let’s dive into Python next to take your coding to the next level. You’re killing it, future developer!

Chapter 3: Introduction to Text-Based Programming with Python

Welcome to the next stage of your coding journey with Introduction to Text-Based Programming with Python, tailored for high school students ready to transition from visual tools to writing actual code. Python is one of the most popular and beginner-friendly programming languages, known for its simplicity and versatility. This chapter marks your entry into text-based coding, equipping you with skills to create powerful programs and solve real-world problems.

Discover why Python is the perfect starting point for new programmers, set up your coding environment, and write your first lines of code. You’ll learn essential concepts like data types and control structures, building a solid foundation for more advanced programming. This hands-on chapter will help you understand how to structure and execute programs with clarity and confidence.

  • Why Python? Features and Uses for Beginners - Explore Python’s simplicity and its wide range of applications.
  • Setting Up Python Environment (IDLE or Online Editors) - Learn how to install and use Python on your device or online.
  • Writing Your First Python Program: Hello World - Create your first program and see it run.
  • Understanding Data Types, Variables, and Basic Operations - Grasp the building blocks of Python programming.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content:
Chapter 3: Introduction to Text-Based Programming with Python

 

Section 1: Why Python? Features and Uses for Beginners

Why Learn Python?

Python is one of the most beginner-friendly programming languages out there, and it’s a fantastic first step into text-based coding for high school students like you. Imagine Python as the “English” of programming languages—its syntax (the way code is written) is simple, readable, and feels almost like writing plain sentences. Unlike other languages with complicated symbols or strict rules, Python lets you focus on solving problems rather than wrestling with confusing code.

Key Features of Python That Make It Awesome:

  • Easy to Read and Write: Python code looks clean and straightforward. For example, to print something on the screen, you just write print("Hello!")—no weird symbols or extra stuff needed!
  • Versatile and Powerful: Python is used everywhere—from creating games (think Minecraft mods) to analyzing data for TikTok trends, building web apps like Instagram, or even programming robots.
  • Huge Community Support: If you’re stuck, millions of Python coders (including other teens) are online to help via forums like Stack Overflow or YouTube tutorials.
  • Free and Open-Source: You don’t need to pay for anything to start coding in Python—it’s completely free to download and use.
  • Cross-Platform: Whether you’re on a Windows PC at school, a Mac at home, or even a Chromebook, Python works everywhere.

    •  

     

Real-World Uses for Beginners:

  • Games: Create simple text-based adventures or use libraries like Pygame to build 2D games.
  • Automation: Write scripts to automate boring tasks, like renaming 100 files on your computer or sending reminder texts.
  • Web Development: Build cool websites or apps with frameworks like Django or Flask.
  • Data Science: Analyze trends (like your favourite Spotify playlists) or make predictions using data.

Fun Fact for Teens:

Did you know that Python was named after the British comedy group “Monty Python”? The creator, Guido van Rossum, wanted a fun, quirky name for the language. So, when you code in Python, you’re part of a community with a sense of humour!

Why It’s Perfect for You:

As a high school student, Python is your ticket to creating projects that impress your friends, teachers, or even future colleges. Start with small programs (like a calculator) and work your way up to bigger ideas (like a chatbot for your group chat). Python gives you the power to turn your imagination into reality while teaching you logical thinking—a skill that’s useful in any career.

 

Section 2: Setting Up Python Environment (IDLE or Online Editors)

Why Do You Need a Coding Environment?

Before you can write Python code, you need a place to write and run it. Think of a coding environment as your “workshop”—it’s where you craft your programs. For beginners, there are two easy ways to get started: installing Python with IDLE (a built-in editor) or using an online editor (no installation needed).

Option 1: Installing Python with IDLE

IDLE (Integrated Development and Learning Environment) comes free with Python and is perfect for beginners. Here’s how to set it up with detailed steps:

  • Download Python:
    • Go to the official website (python.org).
    • Click on “Downloads” and select the latest version for your operating system (Windows, Mac, or Linux). It’s free!
  • Install Python:
    • Run the downloaded installer file.
    • Follow the on-screen instructions. Make sure to check the box that says “Add Python to PATH” during installation (this lets you run Python from anywhere on your computer).
    • Click “Install Now” and wait for the process to complete.
  • Open IDLE:
    • After installation, search for “IDLE” in your computer’s search bar (e.g., Start Menu on Windows).
    • You’ll see two modes:
      • Interactive Shell: A window where you can type and test small bits of code instantly.
      • Editor Window: A place to write longer programs and save them as files (with a .py extension). Access this by clicking File > New File in IDLE.
  • Test It:
    • In the interactive shell, type print("Hello, I’m ready to code!") and press Enter.
    • If it prints your message, your setup is successful!

Option 2: Using Online Editors

If you’re on a shared computer (like at school) or don’t want to install anything, online editors are a lifesaver. They let you code right in your browser. Here’s how to get started with a popular one, Replit:

  • Sign Up for Replit:
    • Go to replit.com.
    • Click “Sign Up” and create a free account using your email or a Google account.
  • Create a New Project:
    • Once logged in, click “+ Create” or “New Repl.”
    • Choose “Python” as the language.
    • Give your project a name (e.g., “MyFirstPython”) and click “Create Repl.”
  • Start Coding:
    • You’ll see a coding area on the left and a run/output area on the right.
    • Type print("Testing Replit!") in the editor and click the green “Run” button to see the output.
  • Save and Share:
    • Your work saves automatically in Replit.
    • Click “Share” to get a link and show your code to friends or teachers.

Other online editors for teens:

  • Trinket (trinket.io): Simple and great for learning with built-in tutorials. Sign up, click “New Trinket,” select Python, and start coding.
  • Google Colab: Awesome for data or AI projects later on. Search for “Google Colab,” sign in with a Google account, and create a new notebook to code.

Practical Tip for Teens:

If you’re using a school computer, check with your IT teacher about installing Python. If it’s not allowed, stick to online editors like Replit—you can code during study hall and show off your projects to friends by sharing a link!

Fun Challenge:

Once your environment is set up (IDLE or online), customize your workspace! In IDLE, change the font or colors under “Options > Configure IDLE.” Online editors like Replit let you pick cool themes (like a dark mode for late-night coding). Make it feel like YOUR space by experimenting with these settings.

 

Section 3: Writing Your First Python Program: Hello World

What Is “Hello World”?

Writing a “Hello World” program is a tradition in coding—it’s the simplest way to test if your setup works and get a taste of writing real code. You’re telling the computer to display the text “Hello, World!” on the screen. Let’s do it with multiple examples!

Example 1: Basic Hello World

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Use IDLE’s editor window (File > New File) or an online editor like Replit.
  • Write the Code: Type the following line exactly as shown:

print("Hello, World!")

  • Save the File (if using IDLE):
    • Go to File > Save As.
    • Name it hello.py and choose a location (like your Desktop).
  • Run the Program:
    • In IDLE, press F5 to run.
    • In Replit, click the “Run” button.
  • See the Output: You should see Hello, World! printed in the output area. Congrats, you’ve written your first Python program!

Output:

Hello, World!

Breaking It Down:

  • print() is a function (a built-in command) that tells Python to display something on the screen.
  • The text inside the quotes ("Hello, World!") is what gets printed. You can change it to anything, like "Yo, I’m a coder now!".
  • Notice there are no semicolons or braces like in other languages—Python keeps it clean.

Example 2: Personalized Greeting

Let’s make it more fun by adding your name. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open a New File or Project: Same as before, in IDLE or online.
  • Write the Code:

print("Hey, I’m [YourName] and I’m learning Python!")

Replace [YourName] with your actual name, e.g., "Hey, I’m Mia and I’m learning Python!"

  • Save (if needed): Name it greeting.py if using IDLE.
  • Run the Program: Use F5 in IDLE or the Run button in Replit.
  • Check Output: See your personalized message!

Output (example):

Hey, I’m Mia and I’m learning Python!

Example 3: Multi-Line Greeting

You can print multiple lines using separate print() statements. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open or Reuse Your Editor: Continue in the same file or start a new one.
  • Write the Code:

print("Welcome to my first program!")

print("Python is awesome!")

print("Let’s code something epic!")

  • Save (if needed): Name it multi_hello.py if using IDLE.
  • Run the Program: Execute as before.
  • See the Output: Each print() creates a new line.

Output:

Welcome to my first program!

Python is awesome!

Let’s code something epic!

Practical Explanation:

These tiny programs teach you two big ideas: (1) how to give instructions to a computer using code, and (2) how to see the result (output). It’s like sending a text message to your computer, and it replies by showing your words. Each example builds confidence in running code and experimenting.

Fun Twist for Teens:

Change the text to something funny or personal, like print("Hey, Python, let’s make a viral game!"). Share the output screenshot with your friends or on social media with #MyFirstCode. Coding is cooler when you make it your own! Bonus: Write a 3-line message to your favorite gamer or influencer and share it.

Troubleshooting Tip:

If nothing prints, check for typos. Python is picky about spelling and capitalization—Print() won’t work; it must be print(). Also, ensure quotes are straight (") not curly (“). If you’re stuck, ask a friend or search “Python print not working” online.

 

Section 4: Understanding Data Types, Variables, and Basic Operations

What Are Data Types and Variables?

In coding, you need to store and work with information—like numbers, text, or true/false values. Data types tell Python what kind of information you’re using, and variables are like labeled boxes where you store that info to use later.

Common Data Types for Beginners:

  • String (str): Text or words, written inside quotes. Example: "Hello" or "I love pizza".
  • Integer (int): Whole numbers, no decimals. Example: 5, -10, 0.
  • Float (float): Numbers with decimals. Example: 3.14, -0.5.
  • Boolean (bool): True or False values, used for decisions. Example: True, False.

Creating Variables:

A variable is a name you give to store data. Think of it as a nickname for a value you can reuse.

  • Syntax: variable_name = value
  • Example:

name = "Alex" # String

age = 16 # Integer

height = 5.9 # Float

is_coder = True # Boolean

Basic Operations:

You can do math or combine data using operators.

  • Math Operators: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide), // (floor division, no decimals), % (remainder), ** (exponent).
  • String Operation: + to join text (concatenation).

Example 1: Simple Math with Variables

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start a new file or project in IDLE or online.
  • Write the Code:

score = 50

bonus = 25

total = score + bonus

print("Total Score:", total)

  • Save (if needed): Name it math_score.py if using IDLE.
  • Run the Program: Use F5 or the Run button.
  • Check Output: See the result of the addition.

Output:

Total Score: 75

Example 2: String Concatenation

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open or Reuse Editor: Continue or start fresh.
  • Write the Code:

first = "High"

second = "School"

full = first + " " + second

print(full)

  • Save (if needed): Name it string_join.py.
  • Run the Program: Execute the code.
  • Check Output: See the combined text.

Output:

High School

Example 3: Mixed Operations for a Fun Calculator

Let’s calculate how many hours you’ve spent gaming this week. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: New file or project.
  • Write the Code:

days_played = 5

hours_per_day = 2.5

total_hours = days_played * hours_per_day

print("I’ve gamed for", total_hours, "hours this week!")

  • Save (if needed): Name it game_hours.py.
  • Run the Program: Check the result.
  • Check Output: See your total gaming hours.

Output:

I’ve gamed for 12.5 hours this week!

Practical Project: Personal Profile Calculator

Let’s write a program to store info about yourself and do some fun calculations. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start a new file or project.
  • Define Variables: Add your name (string), age (integer), and height in feet (float).
  • Calculate Months Lived: Multiply age by 12.
  • Print Results: Use multiple print() statements with concatenated text.
  • Save (if needed): Name it profile_calc.py.
  • Run and Check: See your personalized output.

Code Example:

name = "Jordan"

age = 15

height = 5.8

months_lived = age * 12

print("Hey, I’m " + name + "!")

print("I’ve been alive for " + str(months_lived) + " months.")

print("I’m " + str(height) + " feet tall and ready to code!")

Output:

Hey, I’m Jordan!

I’ve been alive for 180 months.

I’m 5.8 feet tall and ready to code!

Note: We use str() to convert numbers to strings for printing with text.

Additional Project: Snack Budget Calculator

Calculate how many snacks you can buy with your allowance. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start anew.
  • Set Variables: Define your allowance (integer) and snack price (float).
  • Calculate Quantity: Use floor division (//) to find how many snacks you can afford.
  • Calculate Remainder: Use modulo (%) for leftover money.
  • Print Results: Show what you can buy and change left.
  • Save (if needed): Name it snack_budget.py.
  • Run and Check: Verify the math.

Code Example:

allowance = 20

snack_price = 3.50

snacks_you_can_buy = allowance // snack_price

leftover_money = allowance % snack_price

print("With $" + str(allowance) + ", I can buy " + str(snacks_you_can_buy) + " snacks.")

print("I’ll have $" + str(leftover_money) + " left over.")

Output:

With $20, I can buy 5.0 snacks.

I’ll have $2.5 left over.

Interesting Element for Teens:

Turn the profile calculator into a “Future Predictor”! Add a line to calculate your age in 10 years (future_age = age + 10) and print a funny prediction like "In 10 years, I’ll be " + str(future_age) + " and a gaming app millionaire!". Share your output with friends for laughs.

Code Extension:

future_age = age + 10

print("In 10 years, I’ll be " + str(future_age) + " and a gaming app millionaire!")

Practical Tip:

Variable names should be descriptive (like player_score instead of x) so your code makes sense later. Avoid spaces or starting with numbers (e.g., 2score is invalid; use score2 instead).

 

Section 5: Control Structures: If-Else Statements and Loops

What Are Control Structures?

Control structures let your program make decisions and repeat actions—think of them as the “brain” of your code. They’re how you make interactive apps or games that respond to users or handle tasks automatically.

If-Else Statements (Decision Making)

These let your program choose what to do based on conditions.

  • Syntax:

if condition:

# Do this if condition is True

else:

# Do this if condition is False

Example 1: Age Checker for a Game

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start a new file.
  • Set Variable: Define an age value.
  • Write Condition: Use if to check if age meets a requirement.
  • Add Feedback: Print appropriate messages for each case.
  • Save (if needed): Name it age_check.py.
  • Run and Test: See which message appears.

Code Example:

age = 16

if age >= 13:

print("Welcome to the game! You’re old enough.")

else:

print("Sorry, you must be 13 or older to play.")

Output:

Copy

Welcome to the game! You’re old enough.

Explanation: If age is 13 or more, it prints a welcome message; otherwise, it shows a rejection message. Conditions use operators like >= (greater than or equal to), < (less than), == (equals), etc.

Example 2: Grade Evaluator

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: New file or project.
  • Set Variable: Input a test score (0-100).
  • Write Nested Conditions: Use if, elif, and else for multiple grade ranges.
  • Print Result: Output the corresponding letter grade.
  • Save (if needed): Name it grade_eval.py.
  • Run and Test: Try different scores.

Code Example:

score = 85

if score >= 90:

print("Awesome, you got an A!")

elif score >= 80:

print("Nice job, you got a B!")

elif score >= 70:

print("Good effort, you got a C.")

else:

print("Keep studying, better luck next time.")

Output:

Nice job, you got a B!

Loops (Repeating Actions)

Loops repeat code multiple times, saving you from writing the same thing over and over.

Example 3: For Loop - Counting Up

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start fresh.
  • Write Loop: Use for with range() to count from 1 to 5.
  • Print in Loop: Display each number.
  • Save (if needed): Name it count_up.py.
  • Run and Check: See the sequence.

Code Example:

for i in range(1, 6): # Starts at 1, ends before 6

print(i)

Output:

1

2

3

4

5

Example 4: While Loop - Countdown

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: New file.
  • Set Variable: Initialize a starting number.
  • Write Loop: Use while to repeat until condition fails.
  • Update Variable: Decrease the counter each time.
  • Add Final Message: Print something after the loop.
  • Save (if needed): Name it countdown.py.
  • Run and Check: Watch the countdown.

Code Example:

count = 5

while count > 0:

print(count)

count = count - 1 # Decrease by 1 each time

print("Blast off!")

Output:

5

4

3

2

1

Blast off!

Practical Project 1: Guess the Number Game

Let’s build a mini-game where the player guesses a secret number. This combines variables, if-else, and loops. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start a new project.
  • Set Variables: Define a secret number and number of chances.
  • Write Intro: Print a welcome message with instructions.
  • Create Loop: Use while to allow multiple guesses.
  • Get Input: Use input() for guesses and convert to integer.
  • Check Guess: Use if-elif-else to compare guess with secret and give hints.
  • Update Chances: Decrease chances each loop; end if correct or out of chances.
  • Save (if needed): Name it guess_game.py.
  • Run and Play: Test by guessing different numbers.

Code Example:

secret = 7

chances = 3

print("Guess my number (1-10)! You have 3 chances.")

 

while chances > 0:

guess = int(input("Enter your guess: ")) # Convert input to integer

if guess == secret:

print("Woohoo! You got it!")

break # Exit loop if correct

elif guess > secret:

print("Too high! Try again.")

else:

print("Too low! Try again.")

chances = chances - 1

print("Chances left:", chances)

 

if chances == 0 and guess != secret:

print("Game over! The number was", secret)

How It Works:

  • input() gets the player’s guess as text, so int() turns it into a number.
  • The while loop runs until chances hit 0.
  • if-elif-else gives hints, and break stops the loop on a correct guess.
  • Try running it—can you guess the number?

Practical Project 2: Multiplication Table Generator

Create a program to print a multiplication table for any number. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: Start a new file.
  • Get Input: Ask user for a number to multiply.
  • Set Range: Decide how many multiples to show (e.g., 1 to 10).
  • Use For Loop: Iterate through the range and calculate products.
  • Print Results: Show each multiplication step.
  • Save (if needed): Name it multi_table.py.
  • Run and Test: Try different numbers as input.

Code Example:

number = int(input("Enter a number to see its multiplication table: "))

print("Multiplication table for", number)

for i in range(1, 11): # 1 to 10

result = number * i

print(number, "x", i, "=", result)

Output (if input is 3):

Enter a number to see its multiplication table: 3

Multiplication table for 3

3 x 1 = 3

3 x 2 = 6

3 x 3 = 9

3 x 4 = 12

3 x 5 = 15

3 x 6 = 18

3 x 7 = 21

3 x 8 = 24

3 x 9 = 27

3 x 10 = 30

Interesting Element for Teens:

Make the Guess the Number game edgy by adding funny messages! Change the feedback to stuff like "Too high, bro, chill with a lower number!" or "Too low, fam, aim higher!". You can also randomize the secret number using the random module (we’ll cover this later) to make every game unique. Challenge your friends to beat your game in fewer guesses!

Code Extension for Fun Messages:

if guess == secret:

print("Woohoo! You’re a legend!")

break

elif guess > secret:

print("Too high, bro, chill with a lower number!")

else:

print("Too low, fam, aim higher!")

Practical Tip:

Be careful with while loops—if the condition never becomes False (like forgetting to decrease chances), your program will run forever (an “infinite loop”). If this happens, stop it with Ctrl+C in IDLE or by closing the window. Also, always test input() with valid data—typing letters instead of numbers for int(input()) will crash the program unless handled (we’ll learn error handling later).

Fun Challenge:

Modify the Guess the Number game to add a “play again” option. After the game ends, ask "Play again? (yes/no)" using input(), and use an if statement to restart if they say “yes.” This makes your game addictive!

Code Extension for Play Again:

play_again = input("Play again? (yes/no): ")

if play_again == "yes":

chances = 3 # Reset chances

secret = 7 # Or change it

print("Guess my number (1-10)! You have 3 chances.")

# Repeat the while loop here

else:

print("Thanks for playing!")

Additional Challenge Project: Simple To-Do List Counter

Create a program to count tasks you need to do. Step-by-Step Coding Sequence:

  • Open Your Editor: New file.
  • Set Counter: Start with 0 tasks.
  • Use Loop: Ask for tasks until user types “done”.
  • Increment Counter: Add 1 for each task entered.
  • Print Total: Show how many tasks were added.
  • Save (if needed): Name it todo_counter.py.
  • Run and Test: Add a few tasks.

Code Example:

task_count = 0

print("Enter your tasks (type 'done' to finish):")

while True:

task = input("Task: ")

if task == "done":

break

task_count = task_count + 1

print("Task added!")

print("You have", task_count, "tasks to do today!")

Output (example):

Enter your tasks (type 'done' to finish):

Task: Homework

Task added!

Task: Clean room

Task added!

Task: Call friend

Task added!

Task: done

You have 3 tasks to do today!

 

Chapter Wrap-up

By now, you’ve taken your first steps into text-based coding with Python! You’ve learned why Python is awesome, set up your coding space, written your first programs, played with data and variables, and built interactive projects using decisions and loops. Each concept builds on the last, so keep practicing with the multiple examples provided. Coding is like gaming—the more levels you clear, the more skills you unlock!

Final Fun Project Idea for Teens:

Create a “Meme Rating App.” Ask users to input a meme idea (text), then use if-else to rate it as “Lit 🔥”, “Meh 😐”, or “Cringe 💀” based on keywords (like if it contains “dank” or “lol”). Use a loop to rate multiple memes in one go. Share your app with friends and see who comes up with the funniest idea!

Step-by-Step Coding Sequence for Meme Rating App:

  • Open Your Editor: Start a new file.
  • Set Loop: Use while to rate multiple memes until user types “stop”.
  • Get Input: Ask for meme text.
  • Check Keywords: Use if-elif-else with string checks (e.g., "dank" in meme_text).
  • Print Rating: Output a rating based on keywords.
  • Save (if needed): Name it meme_rater.py.
  • Run and Test: Try different meme ideas.

Code Example for Meme Rating App:

print("Enter your meme idea (type 'stop' to end):")

while True:

meme_text = input("Meme idea: ")

if meme_text == "stop":

print("Thanks for rating memes!")

break

if "dank" in meme_text or "lol" in meme_text:

print("Rating: Lit 🔥")

elif "cringe" in meme_text:

print("Rating: Cringe 💀")

else:

print("Rating: Meh 😐")

Output (example):

Enter your meme idea (type 'stop' to end):

Meme idea: This is so dank bro

Rating: Lit 🔥

Meme idea: That old joke is cringe

Rating: Cringe 💀

Meme idea: Just a random thought

Rating: Meh 😐

Meme idea: stop

Thanks for rating memes!

Keep Coding!

Experiment with all the examples, tweak them, break them, and fix them—that’s how you learn. Add your own flair to projects, like funny messages or personal touches. Next chapter, we’ll dive deeper into Python with functions and more complex projects. Drop a funny comment in your code (like # I’m the boss of Python now) to remind yourself how far you’ve come. Let’s code some epic stuff together!
